title: Change the Amount, Watch the Bodies

scenes.tts: A nucleus has no membranes inside it. Yet each chromosome keeps to its own region. Ribosomes are assembled in one place, and splicing factors gather in others. So what holds things apart when there are no walls? One proposal is that some of these bodies form by phase separation. That idea makes predictions you can test.
scenes.visual: A nucleus with territories and bodies, a struck-out membrane, then the question and the proposal.
scenes.narration: A nucleus has no membranes inside it. Yet each chromosome keeps to its own region. Ribosomes are assembled in one place, and splicing factors gather in others. So what holds things apart when there are no walls? One proposal is that some of these bodies form by phase separation. That idea makes predictions you can test.

scenes.tts: A bright spot under the microscope can arise in three ways. In phase separation, molecules demix from their surroundings, as oil separates from vinegar. Or a protein can bind clustered sites, many copies of one sequence in one place. Or it can bridge chromatin, so the fibre collapses into a dense globule. All three make a bright spot. They differ when you change the amount of protein.
scenes.visual: Three nuclei: dots demix into a drop, pile onto clustered sites, or a bead chain collapses; all three glow; an arrow says change the amount.

scenes.tts: Phase separation predicts a threshold. Below the saturation concentration, no bodies form. Above it, extra protein goes into the bodies, and the bodies grow. The concentration outside stays at the threshold. This is a buffered dilute phase.
scenes.visual: A plot of protein outside the bodies against total protein; as the total rises a drop grows in a nucleus while the outside curve goes flat at the threshold.
scenes.narration: Phase separation predicts a threshold. Below the saturation concentration, no bodies form. Above it, extra protein goes into the bodies, and the bodies grow. The concentration outside stays at the threshold. This is a buffered dilute phase.

scenes.tts: Now put in numbers. These data are made up, for illustration. Assume one dense phase at 50 micromolar, and a saturation concentration of 1 micromolar. A simple mass balance gives the fraction of nuclear volume that the dense phase takes up. At totals of 2, 4, and 8 micromolar, bodies fill 2.0, 6.1, then 14.3 percent of the nucleus. The bodies grow sevenfold, while the nucleoplasm stays near 1 micromolar.

scenes.tts: Now test two proteins. For protein A, the nucleoplasm measures 1.0, 1.0, then 1.1 micromolar. That fits. For protein B, it measures 1.5, 2.8, then 5.9. Divide by the totals and you get 0.75, 0.70, then 0.74. Protein B keeps a roughly constant fraction outside the bodies. That fits binding sites better.

scenes.tts: Round shapes, fusion, fluorescence recovery, and hexanediol cannot tell these models apart. Treat the result with care. A protein that fails may still phase separate, as one part of a mixture. A protein that passes has not been shown to need its body. So change the amount of protein, and measure inside and outside the bodies.
scenes.visual: Four observations are set aside, two cautions appear, then three nuclei at rising amounts show what to measure.
